title: Database Concepts
overview: This topic covers why organisations moved from separate data files to relational databases, the vocabulary of the relational model (tuple, attribute, primary, candidate, secondary and foreign keys, referential integrity, indexing), how E-R diagrams document one-to-one, one-to-many and many-to-many relationships, and normalisation to Third Normal Form. Paper 1 regularly gives a scenario, a set of data or a set of tables and asks you to draw the E-R diagram, say whether the tables are in 3NF and justify it, or produce a normalised design with every primary and foreign key identified. Marks come from precise terms applied to the given data, not from general statements.
syllabusPoints: Show understanding of the limitations of using a file-based approach for the storage and retrieval of data.
Describe the features of a relational database that address the limitations of a file-based approach.

Show understanding of and use the terminology associated with a relational database model, including entity, table, record, field, tuple, attribute, primary key, candidate key, secondary key, foreign key, relationship (one-to-many, one-to-one, many-to-many), referential integrity and indexing.
Use an entity-relationship (E-R) diagram to document a database design.
Show understanding of the normalisation process, including First Normal Form (1NF), Second Normal Form (2NF) and Third Normal Form (3NF).
Explain why a given set of database tables are, or are not, in 3NF.
Produce a normalised database design for a description of a database, a given set of data, or a given set of tables.

definitions.definition: The formal name for one row of a relation (table): the set of attribute values stored for a single instance of the entity. Commonly called a record.
A named column of a relation holding one property of the entity, such as MemberName. Commonly called a field. Each attribute value in a tuple must be atomic (a single value or no value).
The attribute, or combination of attributes, chosen to identify each tuple in a table uniquely; every tuple must have a value for it and no two tuples may share that value.
Any attribute, or minimal combination of attributes, that is guaranteed to be unique for every tuple and so could be chosen as the primary key.
A candidate key that was not chosen as the primary key. It is still unique and is often indexed so that tuples can also be searched for quickly by it.
An attribute in one table that refers to the primary key of another table, so that the two tables are linked in a relationship.
The rule, enforced through a foreign key, that a value can only be stored in the foreign key if the same value already exists as a primary key in the table it refers to.

A small secondary structure holding the values of one key attribute in order, each with a pointer to the matching tuple in the main table, so searches on that attribute are much faster than scanning every tuple.
The same data being stored more than once, either within one file or across several files, which wastes storage and creates the risk of inconsistent copies.
A table design in 2NF in which no non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute: every non-key attribute depends on the key, the whole key and nothing but the key.

sections.title: Limitations of a file-based approach
content: In a file-based approach each department or program keeps its own data files, usually text files whose layout is defined by the program that uses them. Imagine a sports centre that keeps one file of member details for the front desk, another for the finance office and another for the coaches. The problems fall into three groups. First, integrity within a file: nothing checks data as it is typed, so a member can be entered twice with slightly different spellings, a required item can be left blank, or a class code can be entered for a class that does not exist. Second, redundancy across files: the member's name and phone number are stored in every department's file, so when the member changes their number only some copies may be updated and the files then contradict each other (data inconsistency). Third, data dependency: each program is written around the exact layout of its file (for example, that the fourth item on each line is the phone number), so adding a new item of data means rewriting the file and every program that reads it, and the files are poorly suited to any new application, such as analysing attendance over several years. A single shared file does not help either, because a file cannot restrict access to part of its contents, so staff who need contact details could also read bank details (a data privacy problem).
bullets: Data redundancy: the same data held in several files, wasting storage and making every change a multi-file job.
Data inconsistency: when only some of the redundant copies are updated, different files give different values for the same fact.
Poor data integrity: no built-in validation or checks when data is entered, so errors, duplicates and references to things that do not exist go undetected.
Data dependency (program-data dependence): programs rely on the file's physical layout, so any change to the data structure forces the programs to be rewritten.
Poor privacy and security: access cannot be controlled for part of a file, so anyone who can open the file can read all of it.
Difficult to share and to use for new purposes: each file suits the program it was built for, so extracting combined data for a new task is slow and complex.

sections.title: Features of a relational database that address these limitations
content: A relational database stores data in a collection of related tables (relations), each holding data about one entity, and all access goes through a database management system (DBMS). Each limitation of the file-based approach has a matching feature. Data about one thing is stored once, in the table for that entity, and other tables refer to it through a key rather than copying it, which removes redundancy and with it the chance of inconsistent copies. Every table has a primary key, and the DBMS refuses a new tuple whose key value already exists, so duplicates cannot be created. Foreign keys give referential integrity: a value cannot be entered that refers to something missing from the linked table. Data types and validation rules defined for each attribute are checked whenever data is entered. Because programs send queries to the DBMS rather than reading files directly, new attributes or tables can be added without rewriting existing programs (data independence), and any combination of tables can be queried for a new purpose. Finally, access rights can be set per user or group and per table, so different staff see only the data they need.
bullets: Redundancy and inconsistency are removed because each fact is stored in one place and linked by keys.
Primary keys guarantee each tuple is unique; foreign keys enforce referential integrity between tables.
Validation (data types, ranges, required fields) is applied centrally, whatever program enters the data.
Programs are independent of the physical storage, so the structure can be extended without breaking them.
Queries can join any related tables, making new uses of the data straightforward.
Access rights can be granted to individual users or groups for individual tables, solving the privacy problem of a single shared file.

examples.label: Redundant file data re-stored as two related tables
examples.content:
File-based data (one line per class booking):
BookingNo | MemberName | MemberPhone | ClassName
1 | O. Haddad | 555-0104 | Yoga
2 | O. Haddad | 555-0104 | Spin
3 | O. Haddad | 555-0104 | Pilates

Problem: O. Haddad's phone number is stored three times. If it changes and only line 1 is edited, lines 2 and 3 are now inconsistent.

Relational design:
Member(MemberID, MemberName, MemberPhone)       primary key MemberID
Booking(BookingNo, ClassName, MemberID)         primary key BookingNo, foreign key MemberID

Member:
MemberID | MemberName | MemberPhone
M104 | O. Haddad | 555-0104

Booking:
BookingNo | ClassName | MemberID
1 | Yoga | M104
2 | Spin | M104
3 | Pilates | M104

The phone number is now stored once, so one edit updates it for every booking. Referential integrity also stops a booking being entered for a MemberID that is not in the Member table.

sections.title: Relational terminology: entity, table, tuple and attribute
content: An entity is a type of thing (a person, object, event or transaction) about which data is stored and of which there are many instances, such as Member or Class. In a relational database each entity becomes a table, which the formal model calls a relation. A table's columns are its attributes (informally, fields) and each row is a tuple (informally, a record) holding the data for one instance of the entity, such as one particular member. A table design is written as the table name followed by its attributes in brackets, with the primary key underlined (or labelled PK in typed answers), for example Member(MemberID, MemberName, MemberPhone). Two principles of the model matter in exam answers: each attribute value in a tuple is atomic, meaning it holds one value or none (never a list), and neither the rows nor the columns have a defined order, which is why data is always retrieved by a query rather than by position.
bullets: Entity = the type of thing (Member); tuple/record = one instance (the row for member M104).
Attribute = field = column; tuple = record = row. Use the formal terms when a question asks for relational terminology.
Atomic values: a MemberPhone attribute holds one number; storing 'Yoga, Spin' in a single ClassName attribute breaks this rule.
Do not confuse a relation (a table) with a relationship (a link between two tables).

sections.title: Primary, candidate and secondary keys
content: Every table must have a primary key: an attribute, or combination of attributes, that has a value in every tuple and whose value is never repeated. The DBMS rejects an insert that would duplicate an existing primary key value, which is how the key guarantees each tuple is unique. Sometimes a table has more than one attribute that is guaranteed unique. For a Member table, both MemberID and a unique EmailAddress might qualify; each is a candidate key. One candidate is chosen as the primary key (usually the short, stable one that never changes, here MemberID) and any candidate not chosen becomes a secondary key, which can still be used, and indexed, to find tuples. Often no natural attribute is guaranteed unique, for example names repeat, so an identifier such as MemberID is created specifically to be the primary key. When no single attribute is unique but a combination is, the primary key is a composite (compound) key, as in a ClassMember table where neither ClassID nor MemberID is unique alone but the pair is.
bullets: Primary key: unique and never empty; one per table (it may be composite).
Candidate key: any attribute or minimal attribute combination that could serve as the primary key.
Secondary key: a candidate key that was not chosen as the primary key (some textbooks also use the phrase for any attribute indexed for searching; the coursebook meaning is the candidate-key one).
Choose a primary key that is guaranteed unique for all possible data, not just the current rows: a name that happens to be unique today is still unsuitable.

sections.title: Foreign keys and referential integrity
content: Tables are linked by a foreign key: an attribute in one table whose values are primary key values of another table. In Class(ClassID, ClassName, Day, InstructorID) the attribute InstructorID is a foreign key referring to the primary key of Instructor(InstructorID, InstructorName). The referenced table must be created first, then the foreign key is declared in the referring table. From then on the DBMS enforces referential integrity: it will not accept an InstructorID in Class unless that value already exists in Instructor, and it will not allow an Instructor tuple to be deleted (or its key changed) while Class tuples still refer to it, unless the change is cascaded. This prevents 'orphan' tuples that point to nothing. A foreign key does not have to be unique in its own table: many classes can share the same InstructorID, which is exactly what makes a one-to-many relationship.
bullets: The foreign key goes in the table on the 'many' side of a one-to-many relationship and refers to the primary key on the 'one' side.
A foreign key may repeat within its table and may be part of a composite primary key (as in a link table).
Referential integrity means every foreign key value matches an existing primary key value in the referenced table.
The foreign key and the primary key it references must have the same data type (and normally the same meaning), even if the names differ.

sections.title: Indexing
content: Finding a tuple by scanning every row of a large table is slow. An index is a separate, much smaller structure associated with one attribute of a table, normally the primary key or a secondary key. It holds that attribute's values in order, each with a pointer to the position of the matching tuple in the main table. To find a tuple, the DBMS searches the ordered index (which can use a fast method such as a binary search or a tree) and follows the pointer straight to the tuple. The DBMS normally indexes the primary key automatically, and further indexes can be created on attributes that are searched or joined on frequently. The cost is extra storage, and slightly slower inserts, updates and deletes, because each index must be updated whenever the indexed data changes.
bullets: Purpose: faster searching and sorting on the indexed attribute, especially for tables with many tuples.
An index contains only the key values and pointers, not the rest of each tuple.
Worth adding to attributes that are searched or used in joins often; not worth it for small tables or rarely searched attributes.
Trade-off: faster retrieval versus extra storage and extra work on every change to the data.

examples.label: An index on the secondary key EmailAddress
examples.content:
Member table (stored in the order members joined):
Row | MemberID | MemberName | EmailAddress
1 | M120 | T. Reyes | treyes@mail.test
2 | M104 | O. Haddad | ohaddad@mail.test
3 | M117 | L. Ortiz | lortiz@mail.test

Index on EmailAddress (sorted, with pointers):
EmailAddress | Row
lortiz@mail.test | 3
ohaddad@mail.test | 2
treyes@mail.test | 1

Searching for ohaddad@mail.test: search the sorted index, find pointer 2, read row 2 directly instead of checking every row of the table.

sections.title: E-R diagrams and relationship types
content: An entity-relationship (E-R) diagram documents a database design before any tables are built. Each entity is drawn as a rectangle containing its name, and each relationship as a line between two entities. The ends of the line show the cardinality: a single line end means 'one', and a crow's foot (three prongs) means 'many'. There are three types of relationship. In a one-to-one (1:1) relationship each instance of A is linked to at most one instance of B and vice versa, such as Member and Locker when each member rents one locker; these are rare and can be implemented with a foreign key on either side. In a one-to-many (1:M) relationship one instance of A is linked to many of B but each B to only one A, such as one Instructor teaching many Classes; the foreign key goes in the 'many' table. In a many-to-many (M:M) relationship each A is linked to many B and each B to many A, such as Member and Class (a member attends many classes, a class has many members). To design an E-R diagram from a scenario: pick the entities (nouns with many instances), decide which pairs are directly related, then decide the cardinality by reading the relationship in both directions, one instance at a time: 'one Instructor teaches many Classes' and 'one Class is taught by one Instructor' gives 1:M. More detailed diagrams also label each relationship with a verb and show the minimum as well as the maximum cardinality (for example, a new class may have zero members so far).
bullets: Always read a relationship both ways, starting each sentence with 'one': one Member attends many Classes; one Class has many Members, so the relationship is M:M.
The crow's foot is drawn at the 'many' end: on a 1:M line between Instructor and Class it touches the Class box.
The entity at the crow's-foot end of a 1:M relationship is the one that will hold the foreign key.
An E-R diagram shows entities and relationships, not every attribute; list attributes and keys separately in a key table or table designs.

examples.label: E-R diagram for a sports centre (text form)
examples.content:
Scenario: Each class is taught by one instructor; an instructor can teach many classes. A member can attend many classes and a class has many members. Each member may rent one locker and each locker is rented by at most one member.

Entities: Instructor, Class, Member, Locker

Relationships (| = one, <  or > = crow's foot / many):
Instructor |------< Class          1:M  one Instructor teaches many Classes; one Class is taught by one Instructor
Class      >------< Member         M:M  one Class has many Members; one Member attends many Classes
Member     |------| Locker         1:1  one Member rents one Locker; one Locker is rented by one Member

The M:M relationship between Class and Member cannot be implemented directly and must be resolved with a link entity (next section).

sections.title: Resolving a many-to-many relationship with a link table
content: A many-to-many relationship cannot be implemented directly. A foreign key attribute holds one value in each tuple, so a single ClassID attribute in Member could not record the several classes that member attends (and storing a list would break the atomic-value rule). Putting a foreign key in both tables fails as well, because each table would have to exist before the other. The solution is to add a link (associative) entity between the two, turning one M:M relationship into two 1:M relationships. For Class and Member the link entity ClassMember holds one tuple for each member in each class. Its primary key is the composite of the two foreign keys (ClassID, MemberID), since neither is unique alone but the pair is, and it is also the natural place for any data that belongs to the pairing itself, such as whether that member has paid for that class. The resulting logical E-R model can be summarised in a key table listing each table with its primary and foreign keys.
bullets: Class >----< Member becomes Class |----< ClassMember >----| Member.
The link table holds a foreign key to each of the original tables; together they usually form its composite primary key.
Attributes that describe the combination (FeePaid, date enrolled, grade) belong in the link table, not in either original table.
Every many end in the logical model is a table that contains a foreign key.

examples.label: Key table for the sports centre logical model
examples.content:
Table | Primary key | Foreign key(s)
Instructor | InstructorID | (none)
Class | ClassID | InstructorID
Member | MemberID | (none)
ClassMember | ClassID + MemberID | ClassID, MemberID
Locker | LockerNo | MemberID

Locker holds MemberID as its foreign key for the 1:1 relationship (it could equally have been LockerNo in Member).

sections.title: The normalisation process: 1NF, 2NF and 3NF
content: Normalisation is a step-by-step technique for turning a list of data items (from a form, a description or an existing table) into a set of table designs with no unnecessary redundancy. Start by listing all the attributes, marking any repeating group: a set of attributes that takes several sets of values while the other attributes have one value each. First Normal Form (1NF): a table is in 1NF when it has a primary key, all attribute values are atomic and there are no repeating groups; to get there, move the repeating group into a new table whose primary key combines the original key (now also a foreign key) with the attribute that identifies each repeat. Second Normal Form (2NF): a 1NF table is in 2NF when every non-key attribute depends on the whole primary key; a partial dependency, where a non-key attribute depends on only part of a composite key, is removed by moving that attribute to a new table keyed by that part. A table with a single-attribute primary key is automatically in 2NF once it is in 1NF. Third Normal Form (3NF): a 2NF table is in 3NF when no non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute; such a non-key (transitive) dependency is removed by moving the dependent attributes to a new table whose primary key is the attribute they depend on, and leaving that attribute behind as a foreign key. Each step splits tables but never loses data: the keys let the original data be rebuilt by joining tables.
bullets: 1NF: remove repeating groups; every table has a primary key and atomic values.
2NF: remove partial dependencies (only possible when the primary key is composite).
3NF: remove non-key dependencies (a non-key attribute determined by another non-key attribute).
Each time an attribute group is moved out, the attribute it depends on stays behind as a foreign key so the link is kept.

examples.label: Worked example: normalising a class register to 3NF
examples.content:
Class register sheets (unnormalised data). Assumptions: each class runs on one day with one instructor; FeePaid records whether that member has paid for that class.

ClassID | ClassName | Day | InstructorID | InstructorName | MemberID | MemberName | MemberPhone | FeePaid
C01 | Yoga | Mon | I3 | P. Nair | M104 | O. Haddad | 555-0104 | Y
    |      |     |    |         | M117 | L. Ortiz  | 555-0117 | N
C02 | Spin | Wed | I3 | P. Nair | M104 | O. Haddad | 555-0104 | Y
    |      |     |    |         | M120 | T. Reyes  | 555-0120 | Y

UNF: (ClassID, ClassName, Day, InstructorID, InstructorName, (MemberID, MemberName, MemberPhone, FeePaid))
The inner brackets mark the repeating group: one class has many members.

STEP 1 - 1NF: move the repeating group to its own table.
Class(ClassID, ClassName, Day, InstructorID, InstructorName)                PK ClassID
ClassMember(ClassID(fk), MemberID, MemberName, MemberPhone, FeePaid)        PK ClassID + MemberID
Class: (C01, Yoga, Mon, I3, P. Nair), (C02, Spin, Wed, I3, P. Nair)
ClassMember: (C01, M104, O. Haddad, 555-0104, Y), (C01, M117, L. Ortiz, 555-0117, N), (C02, M104, O. Haddad, 555-0104, Y), (C02, M120, T. Reyes, 555-0120, Y)
Redundancy left: O. Haddad's name and phone appear twice; P. Nair appears twice.

STEP 2 - 2NF: check each non-key attribute of the composite-key table.
MemberName -> depends on MemberID only (partial dependency)
MemberPhone -> depends on MemberID only (partial dependency)
FeePaid -> depends on ClassID AND MemberID (a member can have paid for one class but not for another) - stays.
Class has a single-attribute key, so it is already in 2NF.
Class(ClassID, ClassName, Day, InstructorID, InstructorName)
Member(MemberID, MemberName, MemberPhone)
ClassMember(ClassID(fk), MemberID(fk), FeePaid)                             PK ClassID + MemberID
Member: (M104, O. Haddad, 555-0104), (M117, L. Ortiz, 555-0117), (M120, T. Reyes, 555-0120)
ClassMember: (C01, M104, Y), (C01, M117, N), (C02, M104, Y), (C02, M120, Y)

STEP 3 - 3NF: look for a non-key attribute that depends on another non-key attribute.
In Class, InstructorName depends on InstructorID, which is not the key (non-key dependency).
Member and ClassMember have none.
Instructor(InstructorID, InstructorName)
Class(ClassID, ClassName, Day, InstructorID(fk))
Member(MemberID, MemberName, MemberPhone)
ClassMember(ClassID(fk), MemberID(fk), FeePaid)
Instructor: (I3, P. Nair)
Class: (C01, Yoga, Mon, I3), (C02, Spin, Wed, I3)

Check: every fact is now stored once (P. Nair once, O. Haddad's phone once), every non-key attribute depends on the key, the whole key and nothing but the key, and joining the four tables on their keys rebuilds the original sheets exactly.

sections.title: Explaining whether tables are in 3NF and producing a normalised design
content: To decide whether a given set of tables is in 3NF, test each table in turn with three questions and quote the attributes involved in your answer. Is there a repeating group or a non-atomic value? If so, it is not in 1NF. Does the table have a composite primary key with a non-key attribute that depends on only part of it? If so, it is not in 2NF. Is there a non-key attribute that depends on another non-key attribute? If so, it is not in 3NF. If a table passes all three it is in 3NF, and the set of tables is in 3NF only if every table is. To produce a normalised design from a written description, pick out the entities and their attributes, decide the relationship between each pair, resolve any many-to-many relationship with a link table, give every table a primary key and place a foreign key at the many end of each 1:M relationship; then check the result against the three questions. From a given set of data or tables, follow the 1NF to 2NF to 3NF steps and state which dependency each split removes.
bullets: Name the exact dependency: 'SubjectName depends only on SubjectCode, part of the composite key' earns the mark; 'it has redundancy' does not.
A table with a single-attribute primary key cannot have a partial dependency, so only non-key dependencies need checking for it.
Write every final table in the form TableName(PK, attributes, FK(fk)) and clearly identify both primary and foreign keys.
State any assumption the design depends on (for example, 'each class has only one instructor').

examples.label: Are these tables in 3NF?
examples.content:
Student(StudentID, StudentName, TutorID, TutorName)               PK StudentID
Result(StudentID, SubjectCode, SubjectName, Grade)                 PK StudentID + SubjectCode

Student: single-attribute key, so no partial dependency. But TutorName depends on TutorID, a non-key attribute -> non-key dependency, so NOT in 3NF.
Result: SubjectName depends only on SubjectCode, part of the composite key -> partial dependency, so NOT in 2NF (and therefore not in 3NF). Grade depends on both StudentID and SubjectCode, which is correct.

3NF design:
Student(StudentID, StudentName, TutorID(fk))
Tutor(TutorID, TutorName)
Result(StudentID(fk), SubjectCode(fk), Grade)       PK StudentID + SubjectCode
Subject(SubjectCode, SubjectName)

examples.label: Normalised design from a description
examples.content:
Description: A vet practice records owners (name, phone) and their pets (name, species). An owner can have several pets; each pet has one owner. Each appointment is for one pet with one vet on a given date and time; a vet sees many appointments.

Entities: Owner, Pet, Vet, Appointment
Relationships: Owner 1:M Pet; Pet 1:M Appointment; Vet 1:M Appointment (no M:M to resolve)

Owner(OwnerID, OwnerName, OwnerPhone)
Pet(PetID, PetName, Species, OwnerID(fk))
Vet(VetID, VetName)
Appointment(AppointmentID, AppDate, AppTime, PetID(fk), VetID(fk))

Check: every table has a single-attribute primary key (so 2NF is automatic) and no non-key attribute determines another (for example, OwnerPhone is stored only in Owner, not in Pet), so the design is in 3NF.

comparisonTable.title: The three normal forms
columns: A table is in this form when
How to fix a table that fails
rows: It has a primary key, every attribute value is atomic and there is no repeating group
Move the repeating group into a new table whose key is the original key (as a foreign key) plus the attribute identifying each repeat
It is in 1NF and every non-key attribute depends on the whole primary key
Partial dependencies on part of a composite key
Move each partially dependent attribute to a new table keyed by the part of the key it depends on
It is in 2NF and no non-key attribute depends on another non-key attribute
Move the dependent attributes to a new table keyed by the attribute they depend on, and keep that attribute as a foreign key

diagram.title: Normalising data to 3NF
nodes: List all attributes; bracket any repeating group (UNF)
1NF: move the repeating group to a new table with a composite key and a foreign key
2NF: move attributes that depend on only part of a composite key
3NF: move attributes that depend on another non-key attribute
Check each table: the key, the whole key and nothing but the key; mark every PK and FK

analysisChains.title: Why a file-based system breaks when the data changes
steps: The finance program reads a member file where the fourth item on each line is the phone number
The centre decides to also store an emergency contact for each member
The file layout has to be rewritten, and every program that reads the file must be changed to match
Meanwhile the front-desk file, which also stores phone numbers, is updated separately and drifts out of step
analysisChains.evaluation: This shows both data dependency and redundancy. In a relational database the new attribute is added once to the Member table through the DBMS, existing queries keep working, and the phone number exists in one place only.

analysisChains.title: Why a many-to-many relationship needs a link table
steps: A member attends several classes and each class has several members
A single foreign key ClassID in Member could hold only one class per member
Storing a list of class IDs in one attribute would break the atomic-value rule of 1NF
A link table ClassMember(ClassID, MemberID) stores one tuple per member per class, turning the M:M into two 1:M relationships
analysisChains.evaluation: The link table's composite key prevents the same member being enrolled twice in the same class, and it gives a proper home to data about the enrolment itself, such as FeePaid.

analysisChains.title: How referential integrity protects a design
steps: Class holds InstructorID as a foreign key referencing Instructor
A user tries to add a class with InstructorID I9, which is not in the Instructor table
The DBMS rejects the insert because the foreign key value has no matching primary key
Later, deleting instructor I3 is also refused while classes C01 and C02 still refer to I3
analysisChains.evaluation: Referential integrity stops orphan records that point to nothing, a check a file-based system cannot make; the cost is that related data must be entered and deleted in the correct order.

examTips: When asked for limitations of a file-based approach, name the problem and its consequence: 'the same data is stored in several files (redundancy), so an update to one copy can leave the others inconsistent'.
When asked for relational features, match each to the limitation it fixes, for example primary key prevents duplicates, foreign key gives referential integrity, data stored once removes redundancy.
On an E-R diagram, put the crow's foot at the 'many' end and make sure each relationship line is between the right pair of entities; resolve M:M with a link entity when a logical model is asked for.
When explaining whether a table is in 3NF, quote the attributes: 'X depends on Y, which is not the primary key' or 'X depends only on part of the composite key (Y)'.

In a normalised design, show every table in the form Table(Key, attributes, ForeignKey) and state which attributes are primary keys and which are foreign keys; a design with no foreign keys cannot be linked.
commonMistakes: Confusing a relation (a table) with a relationship (a link between tables), or an entity (a type of thing) with a tuple (one instance).
Defining a secondary key as 'a second primary key'; it is a candidate key that was not chosen as the primary key.
Putting the foreign key on the 'one' side of a 1:M relationship, or trying to implement an M:M relationship without a link table.
Claiming a table with a single-attribute primary key is not in 2NF; partial dependency is only possible with a composite key.
Removing a dependency in 3NF but forgetting to leave the determining attribute behind as a foreign key, which breaks the link between the tables.
Treating a repeating group as fixed columns (Class1, Class2, Class3) and calling the table normalised; repeated columns are still a repeating group.

quickRecall.question: Give three limitations of a file-based approach.
quickRecall.answer: Any three of: data redundancy; data inconsistency; no built-in validation so poor data integrity; data dependency (programs must be rewritten if file structure changes); no control over access to part of a file; hard to combine data for new uses.

quickRecall.question: What is the difference between a candidate key and a secondary key?
quickRecall.answer: A candidate key is any attribute (or minimal combination) that could be the primary key; a secondary key is a candidate key that was not chosen as the primary key.

quickRecall.question: What is referential integrity?
quickRecall.answer: The rule, enforced by a foreign key, that a value can only be entered in the foreign key if the same value exists as a primary key in the referenced table.

quickRecall.question: What does an index contain and why is it used?
quickRecall.answer: The values of one key attribute in order, each with a pointer to the matching tuple; it makes searching on that attribute much faster than scanning the whole table.

quickRecall.question: How is a many-to-many relationship implemented in a relational database?
quickRecall.answer: With a link table containing a foreign key to each of the two tables, usually combined as its composite primary key, creating two one-to-many relationships.

quickRecall.question: What must be true for a table to be in 2NF?
quickRecall.answer: It is in 1NF and every non-key attribute depends on the whole primary key, so there are no partial dependencies on part of a composite key.

quickRecall.question: What does 3NF remove?
quickRecall.answer: Non-key dependencies: a non-key attribute that depends on another non-key attribute is moved to a new table keyed by that attribute, which stays behind as a foreign key.

quickRecall.question: Is Student(StudentID, StudentName, TutorID, TutorName) in 3NF?
quickRecall.answer: No. TutorName depends on TutorID, which is a non-key attribute; split into Student(StudentID, StudentName, TutorID(fk)) and Tutor(TutorID, TutorName).
